title: Basie's later years, Mercer Ellington's band and a corrupted era
summary: Love laments Basie playing out his days and the Ellington name passed to Mercer, and both note how commercialization lowered standards.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: It is and then, I don't know, like you take Count, a very good friend of mine, and you know the ground he's covered, he knows, but if he can get somebody that just plays all right, because he may have two or three who can do the job, so, so what.
And he doesn't lead his own band, he sees very bad advice from management, we won't say any names, that guide his destiny, and Basie hasn't actively been a

leader for many years.
Basie's a very lonely man on his band stand after having played with Lester Young and Herschel and Doug Clayton and Harry Edison and Jack Washington. (Inaudible).
Jack died the same month as Sam Cooke. (Inaudible)
Basie is just going through the motions. The last time he was here in June, I introduced his band, I was paid to introduce him and present him with a painting that a fellow made, which I played with him in '45, '46, and '47, and it's a disgrace that he would take that band around the world today. I'm saying this is a disgrace that Mercer would take this band around and pass it off as Duke Ellington's band. But that's the way it is today.
Most of the guys in Basie's band-- we were very selective in our day, you could afford to be back in the forties and thirties. You know if you got a man in your band who
couldn't play, all the public would know it. Hey, that saxophone player is not with it; nowadays, who knows.
The whole thing has been corrupted by commercialization and the american dollar. We were fortunate enough to live in a great era of american music.
